text: It’s so hard to judge a book. Sometimes a book only clicks when you’re ready for it. Sometimes you enter a phase in your life that makes you feel lost, and the wisdom of a book turns out to be the perfect map that leads you through it. Round two with The Creative Act . I actually read this one a year ago, when it came out. What’s crazy is that the same pages hit so much harder now. Not because the writing changed, but because of where I am in my own life this time around. That’s what Rick Rubin’s The Creative Act was for me. After almost a year of not making any content, I recently decided to start again. And I hit a wall almost immediately. That’s the phase I picked it back up in. I have a graveyard. Half-built products. Drafts that never got a title. A channel idea I rewrote so many times it never went up. Features I polished for a week that nobody ever asked for. If you saw the folder, you’d think I was lazy. I’m not lazy. I ship constantly. And this isn’t a recent slump. Some of these projects go back ten years. The graveyard has been filling up, quietly, for most of my creative life. The graveyard isn’t full of things I didn’t finish because I ran out of time. It’s full of things I didn’t finish because finishing meant someone could finally look at them and decide. For years I called that perfectionism. High standards. “I just want it to be good before it goes out.” I said it like it was a virtue. It took reading The Creative Act to see it plainly for what it was: fear wearing a nicer outfit. Here are the ideas from the book that finally got me shipping again, and how each one pried a little more fear loose. Separate the 4 Phases of Creation Key Idea: every project moves through four phases, and most things stall because you’re working in the wrong one. Then Rubin gave me the diagnosis for why. He breaks a project into four phases, and getting them confused is usually why things stall. Seeds : you collect ideas, notes, fragments, without deciding if any are good. You’re a collector, not an editor. Experimentation : you play with those seeds, test weird combinations, run tiny experiments without caring how they turn out. Craft : the manual labor of actually building the thing. Finishing : the polish, and the letting go. The mistake that wrecked me for years? I was doing Craft and Finishing during Seeds. The clearest example: I’d sit down to brainstorm, and right there in the middle of gathering, I’d start judging every idea as it came. Killing off the “bad” ones on the spot. I was applying the filter in the exact phase where I should’ve just been opening my mind and collecting. No rules, no editing, just catching whatever showed up. That’s the whole lesson. Gathering and filtering have to be separate steps. You can’t do both at once. When you judge a seed like it’s already a finished thing, you kill it before it ever gets a chance to grow into anything. Then you wonder why you never have good ideas. You had plenty. You just handled them in the wrong phase. So now, when I feel stuck, I ask one thing: what phase am I really in, and what phase am I acting like I’m in? Most of the time, I’m trying to finish something I haven’t even started playing with yet. It’s Just a Snapshot, Not a Scorecard Key Idea: what you make is a record of who you were on the day you made it. It is not a scorecard for your worth as a person. Psychologists have a name for the trap on the other side of this. They call it contingent self-worth, where your sense of value rises and falls with your latest result. Ship something good, you’re a genius. Ship something flat, you’re a fraud. Your whole self hangs on the last thing you made. I lived in that loop for years without noticing. A post did well and I felt untouchable for a day. The next one flopped and I quietly wondered if I’d lost it. Same person, same skills, forty-eight hours apart. The only thing that changed was a number. Rubin’s reframe breaks the loop. A project isn’t a test you pass or fail. It’s a snapshot. Of course something I made two years ago looks rough now. I’ve grown since then. That’s a good sign, not a bad one. Nobody looks at an old photo of themselves and thinks it’s the final word on their face. It’s just where you were standing back then. Your work is the same. It captures a moment, not a verdict. Once It’s Done, Your Relationship With It Is Over Key Idea: the moment you publish something, let it go. Stop gripping it, stop tracking what people say about it, and turn to the next thing. Once a piece is out, it stops being yours. Your job was the making, and the making is done. Holding on after that doesn’t help the work. It just keeps you tethered to something you’ve already finished, refreshing to see who liked it, bracing for who didn’t. That grip is what blocks the next idea from coming. You can’t reach for what’s next while both hands are still wrapped around what’s already out the door. So Rubin’s idea is to treat publishing as the goodbye. You put it out, you let it be what it is, and you move on before the reactions even land. Make the Next Step Too Small to Fail Key Idea: shrink the goal until it’s so small that fear has nothing to grab onto. When a whole project feels too big to face, I don’t try to force my way through the fear. I make the next step tiny instead. Not “finish the post.” Just “write one ugly first line.” Not “ship the feature.” Just “make the button show up on screen.” Fear needs stakes to work. It feeds on “this has to be good, this has to land, people are going to see this.” But there are no stakes in writing one bad sentence you can delete in ten seconds. There’s nothing there to be afraid of. I learned this from running, of all places. On the days I dreaded a run, I stopped telling myself to go do 5K. I just told myself to put my shoes on and step outside. That’s it. That’s the whole goal. And if all I did was walk, that counted too. But here’s the thing: once the shoes are on and I’m out the door, I almost always run. The hard part was never the running. It was the size of the thing I was asking myself to start. Creative work is the same. You take one small step, and then, almost always, the next one feels a little easier. Momentum does the rest. Create for Yourself First Key Idea: make the thing that makes you lean in, and let go of how people react to it. The other trap is harder to admit, because I run content for a living. It’s making things for the reaction instead of for myself. The moment I start building for an audience, an algorithm, or a trend, the work goes thin. Rubin’s answer: follow your own genuine curiosity. Make the thing that makes you lean in, and trust that if you find it compelling, the people who think like you will too. The line I highlighted. That’s not a marketing strategy. It’s the only version of the work that’s actually yours. And it’s the antidote to perfectionism, which is really just an attempt to control the reaction in advance. You’re polishing and polishing because some part of you believes that if you get it perfect enough, you can guarantee how people respond. You can’t. You were never going to. When the work is made for you first, their reaction stops being the point. What changed Here’s the part that matters. Otherwise this is just me talking about my feelings. I started shipping things before I thought they were ready. On purpose. Rough, honest, a little exposed. And the sky didn’t fall. Some of them did nothing. A few connected with people in a way the “perfect” version never would have. Precisely because they were unguarded. The work I was most scared to release turned out to be the work that resonated most. And I’d been sitting on it, out of fear that it wasn’t good enough. The graveyard is still there. But I add to it a lot less now, because I finally understand what was putting things in it. It was never that the work wasn’t ready. It was that I wasn’t ready to be seen. If you’ve got a graveyard of your own, the move isn’t to make the work better. It’s to figure out what phase you’re actually in. Make the thing for yourself. Let it be a record of who you are right now. And ship it, so there’s room for whoever you’re about to become.

The first time I watched I’m Thinking of Ending Things in 2020, I hated the ending. Reading what people were saying about the film gave me the impression it was going to be a “mindfuck” kind of film, and I love those, so I went in totally blind to get the maximum shock factor. But when the ending came, it just didn’t land for me. It felt like this long, careful buildup that never gave me the payoff I was waiting for, and I chalked it up as a pretty but confusing mess and moved on. Then, here we are, six years later, and YouTube’s algorithm drops a video in my feed of a guy doing a nearly two-hour analysis of the film, and it hit me that I’d completely missed the point the first time. What I’d written off as a puzzle with no solution was actually one of the saddest, simplest stories I’d ever seen. Here’s what I took away from it. 1. The Cost of Inaction The entire tragedy traces back to one small moment decades earlier. A young man is at a trivia night in a pub with his friends. Across the room, he notices a woman, and for a moment the whole night narrows down to her. He feels that spark, the small electric pull that says go talk to her. But he waits for the right opening, the perfect line, the moment when it won’t feel awkward. So instead of walking over, he just looks. He keeps glancing at her across the bar, working up a nerve that never comes, and the longer it goes on the worse it gets, because now he’s not a stranger who might say hello, he’s the guy who kept staring and never said a word. Then she gathers her things and leaves, and that’s the end of it. In the only version of this night that survives, she barely registers him at all: not a missed connection, not the one who got away, just a vaguely creepy man who watched her from across a room decades ago. He never even became a person to her. That’s how completely his inaction erased him. He chose safety over a tiny social risk. And really, what stopped him was the fear of being rejected: the dread of walking over, saying something, and being met with a blank look, a polite brush-off, or worst of all, laughter. In that moment, staying silent felt like the safe choice, the way to protect himself from a few seconds of humiliation. But that one hesitation, tiny as it felt, didn’t stay small. A life isn’t shaped by one choice; it’s shaped by thousands of them. String enough of those small “not right now” moments together, one skipped conversation, one unsent message, one room you never crossed, and they quietly bend your entire trajectory. Each one seems harmless on its own, but together they add up to a whole life, the specific narrow life you can only end up with if you keep choosing not to take the risk. For Jake, it metastasized across the decades into profound isolation, until the only relationship he had left was one he invented entirely in his head. This is the film’s real gut-punch, hidden in plain sight: the girlfriend we follow the whole movie was never a real person. Her name, her job, her clothes, even her face keep shifting because she isn’t real, she’s a projection Jake assembled from women he glimpsed and never approached, stitched together with other people’s art, other people’s words, other people’s lives. The one great love of his life is a composite he built alone in the dark, decades after the trivia-night woman walked out the door. The lesson lands like a slap: the sting of possible rejection is microscopic next to the lifelong weight of regret. Honestly, that’s the part that really got under my skin. Watching an old Jake just sitting there, alone and full of regret over a life he never reached for, I couldn’t help but think about my own hesitations, all the times I’ve let fear quietly talk me out of doing something. A message I didn’t send. A conversation I talked myself out of. A girl I couldn’t take my eyes off but never worked up the nerve to talk to. An opportunity I circled but never took, telling myself there’d be a better moment. None of those felt like much in the moment, exactly like Jake’s night at the bar didn’t feel like much. But that’s the whole terrifying point: you never notice the life-defining choices while you’re making them. But in hindsight, they turn out to be the exact forks where a whole life quietly took its shape. 2. No One Is Coming to Save You In the film, Jake spends decades waiting for life to get better on its own. And by the time we see him as an old man, he’s still doing it, still sitting and waiting, as if the change he kept expecting might finally show up if he just holds out a little longer. He hears all the motivational lines about how it’s never too late, how things turn around, how there’s a plan for you, and he’s decided they’re lies. And you can understand why he’s bitter. But that bitterness becomes its own trap, because he uses the emptiness of the clichés as permission to keep doing nothing. That’s the cruel twist of it. He’s not wrong that hope alone is hollow. He’s wrong to conclude that the answer is to stop trying. Hope without action rots. Waiting for change to arrive from the outside is the disease, not the cure, and the only thing that ever actually shifts a life is the person deciding to move first. And that’s the realization I walked away with. Unless I’m genuinely content with where my life is, I can’t just sit around waiting for it to get better on its own, because it won’t. Time passes whether I act or not; the only question is whether I have anything to show for it when it does. Comfort is a quiet thing to drown in. If I want something different, the responsibility is mine. I have to take the action. I have to take the risks and actually make it happen, because no one is coming to do it for me, and the waiting only ever ends one way. And if I’m not willing to do anything about it, then I’ve given up my right to complain about where I end up. The whole thing is on me either way. 3. The Slow Comfort of Giving Up The film ends where it began: on a lone truck sitting in the parking lot of the school where Jake spent his working life. Everything we watched, the girlfriend, the drive, the dinner with his parents, was happening inside his head as he sat in that truck in the middle of a blizzard, slowly freezing to death. The whole film is the last performance of a mind shutting down in the cold. What makes it unbearable is a real detail the story leans on: paradoxical undressing. Here’s how it works. As you freeze, your body pulls blood away from your skin to protect your heart and keep your core warm. But near the end, that system breaks. All that blood rushes back to the surface at once, and suddenly you feel boiling hot even though you’re freezing. So you rip off your clothes to cool down, which just makes you freeze even faster. As strange as it sounds, that’s what people commonly do in the final stages of freezing to death. What struck me watching it was how perfectly this maps onto what Jake did with his whole life. Retreating inward felt like warmth. Staying home, living inside his own head, it all felt like protection, when it was the very thing killing him. That’s what makes it so insidious: the freeze doesn’t announce itself as danger. It arrives disguised as relief, the smart and cozy alternative to the cold hassle of putting yourself out there, right up until the end. The unsettling part is how ordinary this looks from the outside. It isn’t dramatic. It’s a man slowly choosing comfort over connection, over and over, each choice reasonable on its own, until one day the sum of them is a life spent entirely alone. The cold never feels like cold. That’s exactly why it wins. 4. The Comfort of Expecting the Worst Connection can be painful. People can be painful. The film never pretends otherwise, and neither should you. But the pig’s strange monologue and the awkwardness at the ice cream stand keep circling the same idea: the assumption that everyone is out to hurt you is far more dangerous than any actual person. That assumption is what leads Jake to the cold, empty truck. Treating cynicism as armor feels smart and safe, a way to never be let down. But all it really does is guarantee the loneliness you were trying to defend yourself against. You can’t wall yourself off from pain without also walling yourself off from everyone who could have made your life worth living. Thankfully, I’m well past believing this myself, but I’d be lying if I said it never creeps back in. It still shows up now and then, that quiet urge to expect the worst so I don’t have to risk anything. And I’ve met plenty of people who live there permanently. What’s striking is that they genuinely think it makes them the wise one. They forecast that the plan will fail, that the person will flake, that the opportunity is a scam, and they wear that pessimism like insight, as if predicting disaster is the same as understanding the world. But nine times out of ten, the “wisdom” is just a pre-written excuse. It’s a way to talk yourself out of the risk before you ever have to face it, and then call your cowardice foresight. I try to catch myself whenever I hear that voice, because I know exactly where the road it’s on ends. If there’s something to take from this, it’s to get honest about the difference between caution and cowardice, because they sound identical from the inside. Real wisdom weighs a risk and then does something about it; it plans, prepares, and moves anyway. Cynicism just uses the risk as a reason to never move at all. So the next time you catch yourself confidently predicting why something won’t work, ask whether you’re actually protecting yourself or just building a comfortable excuse. Assume the best often enough to give life a chance to surprise you, because a life spent avoiding every disappointment is its own slow disaster, and it’s the one that actually comes true. Say Hello While You Still Can The film isn’t telling you to be reckless. It’s telling you to show up. Ask the question. Say the word. Cross the room. Because the alternative was never safety. The alternative is a man freezing in a parking lot with a head full of scripts he never performed, mourning a life he was too afraid to reach for. I’ll admit I felt a little embarrassed that it took a two-hour breakdown for the message to click. But the guy in the video is generous about it. He doesn’t blame anyone for missing it, because it’s such a dense, slippery film, and he’s honest that he only really got it himself after going back and reading the book. That made me feel better. Some films don’t hand you the meaning; you have to go dig for it. And this one was worth the dig. So take the shot. Send the message, ask the question, cross the room, start the thing you keep circling. Not because it’s guaranteed to work, but because the version of you that never tries is the one who ends up alone in the truck, warming himself on a life that only ever happened in his head. The cold is patient. It waits for the people who keep telling themselves there’ll be a better time. There won’t be. There’s only now, and the room you’re standing in, and whoever is across it. Say hello while you still can.

I want to tell you why I started Gravity . Not the tidy version that fits on a landing page, but the actual thought process, the thing I kept noticing that wouldn’t let me go, the first two people who proved it could work, and the story behind the name. The Thing I Kept Noticing For a while I worked as a marketing virtual assistant to realtors and founders. It was unglamorous work, but it put me on calls with a lot of people, and something started happening that I couldn’t shake. I would get on a call with someone and leave it a little stunned at how good they were. Not good in a vague, motivational-poster way. Good in the specific, earned way that only comes from years of doing a thing until you understand it in your bones. They’d casually drop insights about their field that I’d never heard anyone say out loud. Little tricks of the trade. Ways of seeing their industry that only somebody who had lived inside it for a decade could see. Every one of those conversations lit me up. I’d hang up and think, how does this person exist and I’ve never heard of them? Because here’s the part that started to bother me. These same people, the ones blowing my mind on a Tuesday afternoon call, were not seen as leaders in their field. Not even close. Their reputations were nowhere near the size of their actual expertise. They’d post on LinkedIn every once in a while. And even when they were saying something that clearly signalled mastery, it just sat there. It didn’t land. It wasn’t interesting enough to make anyone stop scrolling. The gap between how good they were and how they came across online was enormous. They were the best-kept secret in their own space. And they didn’t even know it. The Question That Turned Into Gravity What really got me was that these people were still chasing . They were winning clients, sure. But they were doing it the hard way: reaching out, following up, pitching, convincing. Spending energy going to the market instead of the market coming to them. And I kept looking at that and thinking it was backwards. Someone this good shouldn’t have to chase anyone. So I started asking a different question. What if I could flip it? What if the content did the pulling? What if, instead of them reaching out, the right people came looking for them ? That question is the whole reason Gravity exists. Because when content actually communicates real mastery, when it shows the depth instead of just claiming it, something changes. It stops being noise and starts being a signal. And a real signal pulls the right people toward you. You stop introducing yourself and start getting introduced. That’s the job I gave myself. Build that pull for founders who have earned it but never had the time to show it. Take the person who is genuinely brilliant and quietly invisible, and make them the one their market comes looking for. Gravity’s First Two Clients Before Gravity had a name, I was already doing the work. Two of the people I was working with at the time eventually became Gravity’s first two clients. We still work with both of them today. I won’t name them here. Confidentiality is part of how we work at Gravity, and it matters especially with this kind of work. To create content that genuinely sounds like the people we work with, we need to get unusually close to how they think: what they’re seeing inside their businesses, what they believe about their industries, the patterns they’ve picked up after years of doing the work, the conversations they’re having with clients, and sometimes the commercial realities behind those conversations. Some of the best material comes from things they would never think to post themselves. A passing observation on a call. A strong opinion they assumed everyone already knew. A story about a client. Something they’ve learned the hard way over ten years that comes so naturally to them now they don’t even recognize it as expertise. Our job is to find those things. But that kind of access only works when there’s trust. So we protect it. But I can tell you enough about them to show you why Gravity exists. One is the founder of a boutique M&A advisory firm in London. And I remember being a little mind blown almost every time I talked to him. I’d ask what I thought was a fairly straightforward question about selling a business, and twenty minutes later we’d somehow be talking about buyer psychology, deal structure, competitive tension, what happens in a negotiation when one side knows something the other doesn’t, and the tiny signals founders give off that can quietly weaken their position. The interesting part was that he never seemed to think any of this was particularly remarkable. To him, this was just the job. He’d spent years helping business owners navigate acquisitions and exits. He’d seen enough transactions to recognize patterns most founders might only encounter once in their lives. He knew why a founder could have a great business and still leave millions on the table in a sale. He knew the small things buyers notice during diligence that sellers almost always underestimate. He could look at a deal that seemed attractive on paper and tell you where it was likely to fall apart long before anyone else saw it. Sometimes he’d say something almost in passing and I’d stop him. Wait. Say that again. Because what sounded obvious to him absolutely wasn’t obvious to me. And I started realizing that was the opportunity. There was all this expertise sitting inside his head, but almost none of it was making its way onto LinkedIn. If you’d found him there, you wouldn’t have seen the person I was talking to on those calls. His content was professional. Polished. Completely credible. And completely forgettable. It sounded like M&A content: market updates, transaction announcements, the occasional observation about valuations or deal activity. Nothing was wrong with it. But it didn’t communicate mastery. It didn’t give you that feeling I kept getting when I spoke to him: This guy has been in the room. He knows things I don’t know. I’d want him beside me if I were selling my company. That gap fascinated me. Because I knew the person was interesting. I knew the expertise was there. I’d experienced it myself. So the problem wasn’t, How do we make this person more interesting on LinkedIn? It was, How do we make everyone else experience what I experience when I talk to him? That became the work. Instead of asking him for “content ideas,” I started listening differently. I listened for the opinions he’d formed after years around actual transactions. The patterns he’d noticed. The things clients consistently misunderstood. The advice he gave so often that he’d forgotten it wasn’t common knowledge. On one call, he explained that founders often think the negotiation begins when the first offer arrives. His view was that by then, a surprising amount of the negotiation has already happened. How the business was positioned. Which buyers were brought into the process. What information they’d seen. How much competitive tension had been created. All of those things had already shaped what buyers believed the company was worth. And there it was again. Why isn’t this what you’re putting on LinkedIn? That was the content. We started turning insights like that into posts, and people began responding differently. Not just liking them. Asking questions. Sharing them. Starting conversations with him about their own businesses and what an eventual exit might look like. We hadn’t made him more knowledgeable. We hadn’t given him opinions. We hadn’t manufactured some online personality for him. We’d just started letting other people see the person I’d been seeing on those calls. The second client was an estate agent in the UK. Different industry, same experience. I’d get on calls with her and be amazed by how much she noticed. You could mention a neighbourhood and she wouldn’t just know the average price. She’d know the streets, what kind of buyer tended to look there, why one side of an area moved differently from another. She’d know which properties would photograph beautifully but struggle during viewings, and which homes people might scroll past online but fall in love with the second they walked through the door. She knew which renovations sellers routinely wasted money on, and what buyers noticed in the first thirty seconds of a viewing. And again, she’d say these things like they were obvious. They weren’t. They were the product of years of walking into homes, watching buyers react, seeing deals happen and others fall apart, and slowly building an instinct for her market that you couldn’t learn from a property report. But her social media looked like almost every other estate agent’s. New listing. Sold property. Market update. Congratulations to the new homeowners. It told you she was an estate agent. It never told you how good she actually was. So with her, we stopped making the properties the most interesting thing in her content. We made her judgment the interesting thing. Instead of simply posting another listing, we’d talk about what she noticed about it. Why she thought a certain kind of buyer would want it. What the seller had done right. What she would have changed before bringing it to market. Her content stopped saying I’m an estate agent and started showing people this is how I see the market. And that changed the conversations around her. Homeowners started asking for her opinion before they were ready to sell. People who’d been quietly considering putting their homes on the market reached out. Some conversations no longer began with her trying to convince someone she was the right agent. They began with trust already there. These were two completely different people in two completely different industries. One advising founders on M&A transactions in London. The other helping people buy and sell homes in the UK. But they had exactly the same problem. The people I met on those calls were far more impressive than the people I saw online. And that became the thing I couldn’t unsee. I didn’t need to make them more interesting. I didn’t need to manufacture expertise or turn them into “personal brands.” The mastery was already there. My job was to find it, pull it out, and communicate it well enough that someone scrolling LinkedIn could feel a little of what I felt sitting across from them on a call. That became the foundation of Gravity. So Gravity wasn’t built around a theory I wanted to test. It was built around people I’d already worked with, people whose expertise had already blown me away, and a problem I knew we could solve: Make the person the market sees as impressive as the person you meet in the room. Eventually, I just gave that work a name. Why I Chose the Name Gravity I called it Gravity because that’s the most honest word I had for what I was actually trying to create. Part of it came from something I just couldn’t stop thinking about. There are founders and thought leaders I admire who have built these big followings, and when you watch them from the outside, opportunities just seem to come to them. Doors open on their own. The right people show up. They’ve somehow built this whole world around themselves, and everything drifts toward it. It started to feel less like they were going out and getting these things and more like they had a gravitational field, quietly pulling people and opportunities into their orbit. And that’s the thing about gravity. It doesn’t chase anything. It doesn’t reach out, doesn’t push, doesn’t convince. It just is , and because of what it is, things move toward it. The pull isn’t an effort. It’s a property of the thing itself. That’s exactly what real expertise should do. When you’ve built up genuine weight in your field, years of it, the depth should create its own pull. People should feel drawn in. The problem is that most founders have the weight but none of the pull, because nobody can see it. It’s locked inside their heads and their calls and their day-to-day work, and it never makes it out into the world where anyone can feel it. So Gravity is about making that depth visible. Taking what’s already there, the real substance a founder has spent years building, and expressing it clearly enough that it starts doing what real depth is supposed to do: pull. The name is a promise, in a way. Content that communicates real mastery has a gravitational pull. It brings the right people toward you. If you’re the best-kept secret in your space, the fix isn’t to shout louder or chase harder. It’s to finally let the weight of what you know be felt. That’s the concept. That’s the name. And that’s why I built it. How All My Struggles Led Me Here Looking back at those two clients, I can see I was doing three specific things without ever really naming them. I was listening for the expertise they didn’t know they had. I was pulling it out and shaping it into something that could actually earn attention. And I was sweating the words until it sounded like them at their best. Here’s the strange part. I never set out to learn any of those things for this. Every one of them came from somewhere else entirely, and I had no idea at the time that they were preparing me for this. The listening, the client sense, the ability to sit across from a founder and understand how they think, that came from eleven years in marketing, six of them running Partizan , my agency, leading a team and working with big companies. That gave me the foundation: how to work with clients, how to think about a brand, how to run creative work end to end. But if I’m honest, it didn’t give me the thing that matters most here. Back then I couldn’t yet make every word earn its place. I could get the work done. The precision came later. Knowing how to get attention and keep it, that came from Brand Origins , a podcast and YouTube channel I started about the histories behind brands. When you’re making content that has to survive the scroll, you learn fast what a strong hook actually is, what makes someone stop, and what keeps them watching once you have them. You either figure out how to earn attention or nobody watches. That’s the exact skill that turns a founder’s insight into something people actually read. And the word-level obsession, the part where I’ll sit with a single sentence until it’s right, that came from two years in a copywriting role. That’s what made me detail-oriented at the level this work demands. Learning to feel the difference one word makes, to understand that precision isn’t decoration, it’s the whole point. It’s a little crazy how that works. Life keeps handing you experiences you have no idea you’ll need, quietly preparing you for opportunities you can’t even see yet. The agency years, the channel, the copywriting, none of it felt like it was pointing anywhere in particular at the time. Now I can see it was all pointing here. The Founders Gravity Is Looking For Those first two clients taught me something else about the kind of people I want Gravity to work with. I’m looking for the person who gets more interesting the longer you talk to them. The founder who’s spent years getting exceptionally good at something, but whose reputation hasn’t caught up with their ability yet. The person who can say something almost casually in conversation that makes me stop and think, Wait. Say that again. That’s the feeling I’m looking for. Because Gravity only works when there’s something real underneath it. We can find the stories. We can pull out the ideas. We can sharpen the thinking, package it, and make it interesting enough to earn attention. But we can’t manufacture mastery. And I don’t want to. The whole point of Gravity is to take expertise that’s already there and make it visible. So if you’ve built something real, you know your field in your bones, and you’re still somehow one of the best-kept secrets in your space, you’re exactly the kind of person we built Gravity for. You already have the weight. Our job is to help the market feel the pull. And I think that’s what excites me most about where Gravity goes from here. There are so many people out there who are quietly exceptional at what they do. People who’ve spent ten, fifteen, twenty years getting good at something, but who haven’t figured out how to make the rest of the world see what the people closest to them already know. I keep thinking about how many of them I haven’t met yet. How many conversations are still ahead of me where someone says something almost casually and I have to stop them and say, Wait. Say that again. That’s the part I’m looking forward to. I don’t know exactly how big Gravity will become or where all of this will lead. I’m still early enough in the journey that a lot of it is unknown. But I know the feeling I’m chasing. I’ve felt it in those conversations. I’ve seen what happens when someone’s real expertise finally makes it out of the room and into the world. And I want to keep building a company that helps more of that happen. Maybe, years from now, I’ll look back at those first two clients and realize that was the beginning of something much bigger than I could see at the time. I hope so. For now, I’m just excited to find the next person who makes me say: Wait. Say that again.

This week I scrolled ten years back through a Facebook page I’d forgotten I still had, the old page for Partizan , my first company. And I found a younger version of me already chasing everything I’m chasing now. A bunch of dots I never knew were connected, quietly lining up. Same obsessions. Same way of thinking about brands, about fear, about doing the thing anyway. I’ve apparently been writing the same post for a decade haha! So I figured, you know what, now that we’re here, might as well take you back to the origin story of my first company. Why we launched Partizan Before I wrote a single line of code, I ran an agency. It was 2015 and I was fresh out of university. I knew I wanted to start a business. I just had no idea what. What I did have was an obsession. I was completely fascinated by branding and marketing, by how the careful precision of words and a genuinely good story could bring a simple product to life. A lot of that came from one of my mentors in college who got me hooked on it. I got so fascinated with the world of branding that Fully Booked became one of my go-to hangouts whenever I was at the mall, and buying books turned into one of my biggest expenses. The more I dug into that world, the more I thought: maybe this is something I could actually do. Most of my friends were opening restaurants, bakeshops, or diving into their family businesses. Well, I didn’t have that option, and I didn’t have any capital haha. But what I did have was this obsession, one that had quietly, over time, evolved into a real set of skills. So I figured, why not find a way to make money from this? A branding and marketing agency was the obvious answer. And the timing felt right. Back then, hardly any brands were taking Facebook seriously as a way to market themselves. A lot of them didn’t even have pages yet, and the ones that did were posting horrifically designed posters and random photos that were never going to help them sell anything. So the pitch was simple: I’d help brands nail their branding and positioning, look sharper on social media, and turn that attention into sales. And that was it. I had my idea. A branding and social media agency. Now it just needed a name. Why “Partizan” The name came from Seth Godin, one of the figures who influenced me most back then. I read everything of his I could get my hands on, Purple Cow, The Dip, Linchpin, and of course Tribes, and I was subscribed to his newsletter too. I still vividly remember reading Tribes one rainy afternoon, parked in my car by the side of the road in Tigbauan, under a tree. In it, he reclaims the word “partisan” from its negative political baggage. A partisan, in his sense, is someone so fully committed to a cause that the commitment itself becomes the thing people are drawn to. And there’s another image the word brings up for me, especially as someone who’s a big nerd for World War II era history: the Partisans, the resistance fighters who operated against the Nazis under impossible odds. People who, despite everything stacked against them, still found the courage to take action anyway. Both meanings, the devoted supporter and the resistance fighter, come from the same idea, taking a side and giving yourself to it fully. That’s why the word means what it means. The commitment, the conviction, the refusal to sit in the safe middle ground of a cause, that was the whole point of it. That image, people rallying to something they believe in and refusing to back down, was exactly what I wanted the name to carry. That idea hit me hard because with this lens, when I took a second look at Nike, Apple, and even Coca-Cola, even if you don’t like these brands, when you look beyond the ads and the taglines, you realize that they’ve managed to build their brands around conviction. They managed to rally people around a single idea. People don’t rally around lukewarm. They rally around someone who has planted a flag and refuses to move off it. As Godin put it, if you’re a middle-of-the-roader, you don’t bother joining a tribe. Playing it safe, trying to be for everyone, being agreeable to the point of blandness, that’s the actual risk. It makes you forgettable. Commitment, the willingness to stand for something and alienate the people it’s not for, is what makes you magnetic. That was the standard I wanted the agency to live by, and the standard I wanted for the brands we worked with. People who were genuinely obsessed with what they were building, who we could help find the ones who’d rally around it. So I took the word, swapped the “s” for a “z” because it looked and sounded better and was easier to make our own, and Partizan was born. Looking back, the name was the mission. Everything we posted was some version of it: find what you’re obsessed with, commit to it fully, and the right people will come. The premise: purpose-driven brands only Bayani Brew, shot in the rice fields. January 2017. From day one, Partizan worked only with purpose-driven brands. Social enterprises, non-profits, founders using business to make some kind of dent. Not a positioning gimmick, it’s genuinely what we cared about, and the feed proves it: scroll back far enough and it’s post after post about social enterprises and movements. Which brings me to one of our very first clients: Bayani Brew. Bayani Brew is the social enterprise from Gawad Kalinga’s Enchanted Farm, exactly the kind of brand Partizan was built for. We ran their social media. And one experience from that time stuck with me. We needed better photos for Bayani Brew, so one Saturday we headed out at around 6:30 in the morning, stopped by the market to buy ingredients to use as props, then drove out to a quiet barangay road, one that barely saw any traffic, running through the rice fields. We picked a spot, set up, and took the shots right there. Three of the flavors, same morning, same roadside. That set the tone for everything after. Working with the Breadwinner: Angelina Angelina Super Loaf, from one of our outdoor product shoots. Now comes one of my favorite parts of Partizan’s journey ever: working with Angelina. Angelina Bakeshop is the biggest white loaf bread brand in the Visayas, and probably in Mindanao next. They’re on the shelves of practically every supermarket in the region, and they recently expanded to Cebu. And by reputation, in the places Angelina enters, the bread brand that dominates Luzon is said to slip to number two. The work with Angelina was intense, but honestly, it was the most fun we’ve had working with a client, because Ted was awesome. It didn’t feel like work most of the time because we all just vibed. One idea from the COVID season still stands out. We started making timely, relevant posts for Angelina about the strange new habits people were picking up in lockdown. We were watching social media closely, catching the trends while they were still rising, and turning them into content fast. One of those became one of the most shared posts we ever made. What was inspiring about our time with Angelina was realizing that a family-owned local brand can fight beyond its weight-class and knockout a bread brand that dominated Southeast Asia, and all it required was the hands-on commitment and obsession to detail of the family behind it. At its peak, Partizan grew into a team of 10 people in one room, working with 50+ brands over the years. Angelina Buttered Toasts. August 2018. A billboard we designed for Angelina. December 2019. Then COVID hit I’ll keep this short, because it’s really a story for another time. COVID hammered us. An agency built on close, hands-on work with growing brands is a hard thing to hold together when the whole economy freezes and your clients are fighting to survive. Partizan didn’t make it through the way I’d hoped. But it pushed me toward something I’d been doing on the side for years: the writing, the content, the storytelling. I went all-in on Brand Origins full time. And that turn, from running an agency to building an audience, is what eventually led to everything I do now. That’s the short version. The full one is for another day. Hindsight is 20/20 Steve Jobs said it best in his Stanford commencement speech: you can’t connect the dots looking forward, only looking backward. That’s exactly how this feels. Because looking back, I realized that a lot of what I’m doing now are things I already enjoyed doing back then, or things I was already thinking about that far into the past. I mean, think about it. Partizan was the creative outlet of my obsession with branding, with building brands on stories that people rallied around. I was already writing about how to find your brand’s tone of voice and how to dig out a brand’s real purpose way back in 2015, and the 12 brand archetypes a few years after that. That’s the exact same thing I’m doing now with Gravity . And as early as 2018 I was writing specifically about lead generation for real estate companies . Which is funny, because VendorScout , the software I made that helps realtors find and manage their vendors, turns out to be me circling that exact world, real estate, seven years before I actually built anything for it. The purpose-driven brand work, helping founders find the authentic thing they should be saying, is now Heatseeker : the engine I built that finds the conversations a founder can actually speak to and hands them the angles. Same instinct. Different tool. And the writing never stopped either. That same fascination with brands and their stories eventually led me to Brand Origins , and it’s the same thread running through the posts I write now. Same voice, ten years of it. The best part? The version of me back in 2015 was only dreaming of being able to build software himself. And here I am now, building my ideas out on the same day I think of them . The ideas were always there. I finally caught up to them. If you’d told that 2015 version of me that everything he’d go on to build was already hiding inside the work he was doing right then, he wouldn’t have believed you. I guess everything just falls into place in its own right time, huh?

It’s a special kind of hell being a person who comes up with a lot of ideas and not having the skills to build them. I’d get a burst of inspiration, some amazing idea, and I’d note it down. This is what I’m looking at most mornings. Then it would just sit there in my notes for weeks, months, years, never seeing the light of day. I could hire someone else to build it, but that gets too expensive, at least for a raw idea I hadn’t even tested. So eventually I just stopped letting myself have the ideas in the first place, lol. I lived with that for a long time. Until I got tired of living with it. Turns out “not even trying” gets boring too. So I learned how to build. Now when something is on my mind, I can just make it. What a time to be alive! That’s the most fun I’ve ever had working. Where Heatseeker came from Heatseeker came straight out of that. I run Gravity, where I create content for founders. And I kept hitting the same wall, every week, with every client: what do we make content about this week that’s actually relevant to them? The answer was always out there. Somewhere on Reddit, a thread was blowing up on my client’s exact topic. Somewhere in a newsletter, there’s an interesting discussion they could really add value to. But I can’t read the whole internet every day. So I’d miss almost all of it, and end up staring at a blank page instead. So I built the first version of Heatseeker. Back then it did one thing: it scoured Reddit for conversations blowing up in my client’s world and flagged the ones they’d have something worth saying about. It worked. And the moment it worked, the questions started stacking up. What it turned into What if it wasn’t just Reddit? What if it watched everywhere people talk, all at once? And what if AI did the filtering, so nothing came back that the person couldn’t speak to authentically? That’s what Heatseeker turned into. Every day it scours Reddit, X, LinkedIn, newsletters, YouTube, and TikTok for content that’s trending and blowing up right now. Then an AI profile-matching system I built grades every piece against a specific client profile and filters down to the ones that person could authentically talk about and remix into their own version. For each one, it hands back 3 to 4 angles for the remix. Ideation goes from a blank page to picking from a short list of things you’re already qualified to say. Right now it’s a working prototype, not a polished product. It’s an internal tool I run for my own ventures and my Gravity clients. But it’s real, it works, and it’s changed how content gets made: nobody starts from a blank page anymore. It’s just such a nice feeling, being able to build. To have something in your head in the morning and see it running in front of you by the afternoon is still wild to me. I’ll keep building, and I’ll post updates here along the way. I procrastinated for an entire year before making content again. I thought I was lazy. Turns out I was just scared. I envied people who could show up every day with ease, like it was nothing, and I kept beating myself up for not being able to do the same. But then I realized it wasn't a work ethic problem. I was working hard on plenty of other things, just not the one that required me to show up with my name and face attached to it. That's when it hit me. This wasn't laziness. It was fear, plain and simple. I was afraid people wouldn't like what I made, and too afraid to even admit it. The first time, I set the bar on the floor Seven years ago, I decided to finally make content for the first time. I started a podcast and YouTube channel called Brand Origins. It was my first time recording a podcast and my first time showing up on camera. As a shy introvert, this was my nightmare, showing my face for thousands of people to judge. But I remember how I got myself to do it. I told myself I only had one goal. Not to make great work, not to go viral, not to rack up views. Just to MAKE something. It didn't matter if no one watched. My job was just to create one episode after another and improve along the way. For now, the goal was just to get started. Because the bar was so low, just create one episode, showing up felt doable. So I became consistent, and over time Brand Origins grew into something real. People were actually listening to the podcast and watching the videos. Coming back is harder than starting Then, at some point, I had to stop. Life happened, some plans got put on hold, and I stepped away from making content for a while. But the stars aligned again, giving me a shot to make content once more. And for some reason, I couldn't get myself to start. Because coming back after building something real is different than starting from zero. Somewhere along the way, I'd built up an expectation that everything I make now has to be great. The worst part is, I don't even think anyone expects that from me. It's just my self-esteem, my insecurities, and negative self-talk putting that imaginary pressure on myself. And when you strip it all down, it's just fear. Fear of looking like I don't know what I'm doing. Fear of making mistakes. Fear of judgment. Perfectionism is just fear in high heels Fear can be deceiving too. It often hides as perfectionism. "I need this to be perfect," we tell ourselves. But remember what Elizabeth Gilbert said: "Perfectionism is just fear in high heels." That fear is exactly why it took me so long to create again. I just needed to remember what I already knew: sit down, start typing, do the work, and most importantly, NOT WORRY ABOUT THE OUTCOME. So if you're stuck staring at a blank page, you're not lazy. You're scared. And that's okay. We all are. I'm scared publishing this too, but writing it down already made it feel less scary. Maybe that's the whole trick. Accept that you're scared, and do it anyway. The takeaway: start before you feel ready. The fear never fully goes away, you just stop waiting for it to.

The short answer Tarzan bubble gum is made by Philip Sweets Manufacturing Co., Inc., a family candy company that has been running since 1949, originally out of Malabon. It launched Tarzan in 1965, after its first hit, Texas bubble gum, in the early 1960s. Sales faded for decades. Then a nephew working at the factory called into Conan O’Brien’s podcast in November 2024 and asked for marketing help. In October 2025 Conan showed up at the factory and put himself on a billboard on EDSA in a loincloth. The whole thing aired as the season finale of Conan O’Brien Must Go on September 11, 2026. I watched the Philippines episode of Conan O’Brien Must Go the way I watch anything Conan does, which is immediately. I have been a fan for years. I was mostly there for the jeepneys and the balut. Then he walked into a candy factory in Manila, held up a pack of Tarzan bubble gum, and I sat up. Tarzan. I had not thought about that gum in years. I remember the wrapper. I remember it being harder to chew than gum has any business being, and I remember the flavor that I could never quite name as a kid. What I did not remember, because I genuinely assumed otherwise, is that the company is still around. Somewhere along the way I filed Tarzan under things that quietly disappeared. Turns out it never left. It has been running since 1949. So I went digging, and the story is better than the billboard. A man asked a talk show host for free advertising, and got it. Here is who actually makes Tarzan, what else they make, how old the company really is, and my honest read on whether any of this saves them. Sources are linked inline. Advertisement Who Makes Tarzan Bubble Gum? The company is Philip Sweets Manufacturing Tarzan is made by Philip Sweets Manufacturing Co., Inc., which shortens itself to PHISMAN and brands its candy as Philip’s. The company dates itself to 1949 and is still family run. Its original plant was on Isabel Avenue, since renamed Gov. W. Pascual Street, in Northern Hills, Malabon ( Isa Munang Patalastas ). Business directories still list the company on Gov. W. Pascual Avenue, and its Facebook page now shows a Quezon City base. There is no corporate website, no press office, no investor deck. There is a Facebook page, an Instagram account , and a Yahoo email address. That detail matters later. Texas came first, Tarzan came second The company’s first real hit was not Tarzan. It was Texas, a pink square of bubble gum wrapped in waxed paper, sold to schoolkids through the 1960s. It cost one centavo a piece, and five centavos bought six of them. Tarzan followed in 1965 ( Isa Munang Patalastas ). Both names were borrowed from American pop culture, which was the marketing logic of the era. Texas was named after the state. Tarzan was named after the jungle character, which gave a one-centavo chew a bit of adventure. In sari-sari stores, Tarzan became the local answer to Bazooka. Bazooka had comic strips in the wrapper. Tarzan had colored wrappers and a cola flavor with a hint of cinnamon, and a texture tough enough that blowing an actual bubble took commitment. ELI5 A family in Malabon has been making candy since 1949. They made a pink gum called Texas, then a cola-flavored gum called Tarzan. Both were one centavo. Kids loved them. Then it went quiet Both brands faded for years. In the 2010s the company brought Texas back with updated packaging, and Tarzan returned to shelves alongside it. That relaunch found baby boomers and older millennials, the people who remembered the taste. I was apparently supposed to be one of them, and I missed it entirely, which tells you something about how loud the relaunch was. Which is exactly the problem. When Charles de Guia, the mechanical engineer who works at the family factory, described the business on Conan’s podcast, he said the customer base was mostly people aged 50 to 60 ( PhilSTAR Life ). A nostalgia brand whose buyers are aging out is a brand with a clock on it. He also described what the factory used to be, in the sentence that makes the whole story land: “sobrang lakas daw nung candy factory, like 24/7 tumatakbo and may daily deliveries. Right now, hindi na siya ganon” ( GMA News ). How Conan O’Brien Ended Up on an EDSA Billboard He applied to a podcast in May 2024 Conan O’Brien Needs a Friend has a recurring segment where a listener gets a call with Conan. Charles de Guia applied in May 2024. His stated reason was not to meet a celebrity. It was, in his words, that “we could use a bit of advertising, parang marketing exposure” ( GMA News ). Six months later he got the call. The episode went out on November 21, 2024, titled “Charles and the Chocolate Factory” , described on Team Coco’s own site as Conan talking to Charles in Manila about working as a mechanical engineer in an unpopular candy factory. Conan said on air that he wanted to turn things around and make it the biggest candy company in the Philippines ( PhilSTAR Life ). Talk show hosts say things like that every week. This one meant it. The crew called back in July 2025 Conan’s team reached out about filming. On October 15, 2025, Conan and the crew arrived at the factory, about an hour late because of traffic, which is the most Manila detail in the entire story. He drew a doodle at Charles’s desk and signed it, signed a Conan Funko Pop, and left a mug with a note ( GMA News ; GMA Entertainment ). Then came the actual payoff. A billboard went up at EDSA-Guadalupe showing Conan in a cowboy hat, a leopard print loincloth and photoshopped abs, swinging on a vine, holding packs of Tarzan and Texas. The tagline: “ME LOVE GUM, PARDNER.” It was up in October 2025 ( The Chronicle PH ). Conan’s own summary on Instagram: “Visited my fan Charles’ candy factory and lost my f-ing mind.” Charles posted back: “Still chewing on how surreal today was. Love you, Conan!” ( GMA Entertainment ). It aired almost a year later The factory visit became part of “The Philippines,” the fourth and final episode of season 3 of Conan O’Brien Must Go , which aired on HBO and HBO Max on September 11, 2026, September 12 in Philippine time ( Wikipedia ; Rolling Stone Philippines ). The rest of the episode has him playing a medallion-stealing villain on the police drama Sanggang-Dikit FR , touring Intramuros on a bamboo bicycle, getting fitted for a barong, working the front desk at a hotel in Tanauan, eating balut, and shopping for an island. ELI5 A guy who works at his family’s candy factory called into a podcast and asked a famous comedian for free advertising. Almost a year later, the comedian flew to Manila, visited the factory, and put himself on a giant billboard for them. It aired on TV in September 2026. What Else Does Philip Sweets Make? Fewer things than you would guess. This is not a company with fifty SKUs. The full lineup on Philippine grocery shelves is bubble gum and caramel, and that is basically it. Product What it is Sizes and typical price Tarzan Bubble Gum (Original) The cola-and-cinnamon chew from 1965, in colored wrappers 105g about ₱28.25; 265g (50 pieces) about ₱68.50 Tarzan Bubble Gum Cool Mint The mint version, the one most often stocked online 105g about ₱28.25; also sold in 20s packs Texas Bubble Gum The original 1960s pink square, chewy and minty 150g (about 40 pieces) around ₱31; larger pack around ₱75.50 Philip’s Classic Caramel The sticky caramel candy people joke could pull out dentures About ₱53 for the standard pack Philip’s Coffee Caramel Coffee flavored version of the caramel 150g about ₱31; 375g (100 pieces) about ₱75.50 Philip’s Caramel Fruit Flavor Fruit flavored caramel, the newest of the three 75g (25 pieces) about ₱17 Prices above are shelf prices listed by Sta. Lucia Grocers and will vary by store. The caramels ran through sari-sari stores and school canteens from the 1960s into the 1990s, in classic and coffee, before the fruit version was added. So the answer to “what else do they make” is: two gums and three caramels. Six products, if you count Tarzan Original and Cool Mint separately. A company that has survived 77 years on roughly six things. Can a Billboard Actually Save It? Here is where I stop reporting and start guessing, so treat this part as opinion. What Conan gave Philip Sweets is genuinely valuable and genuinely incomplete. Awareness is the top of a funnel. It is the part most small manufacturers cannot buy. A billboard on EDSA-Guadalupe plus a season finale on HBO Max plus a week of Philippine news coverage is more attention than this company has had since the 1970s, and it cost them nothing. But attention converts into revenue through distribution, and distribution is the part nobody films. If a 28-year-old sees the billboard, remembers the gum from their lolo’s store, and then cannot find it at the nearest convenience store, the attention evaporates. Tarzan is stocked in major supermarkets and on Shopee and Lazada, which is real, but it is not the same as being in the impulse-buy position at the counter where gum is actually sold. The second gap is that the brand’s own channels are thin. A Facebook page and an Instagram account with a Yahoo contact address is not a place to send a spike of national curiosity. The moment when everyone is searching for you is the moment you need somewhere for them to land. None of which takes away from the thing that actually happened here. A guy in Malabon looked at a business that used to run 24/7 and decided the bottleneck was that nobody knew about it anymore. Then he did the only cheap thing available to him, which was to ask. That instinct is worth more than the billboard. And it worked on me, and I have never once driven past that billboard. I watched an episode, remembered a wrapper, and went and read everything I could find about a candy company I assumed was dead. That is the whole job of the top of a funnel. The part that is still on them is what happens when the next person who remembers Tarzan goes looking for it and has nowhere good to land. Where to Buy Tarzan Bubble Gum Major Philippine supermarkets carry it, and the company itself has said on Facebook that Tarzan is “available in most major supermarkets.” Online, both Tarzan and Texas are listed on Shopee and Lazada , usually in 105g and 265g packs. For wholesale or bulk, the company lists a landline and the email philipsweets@yahoo.com in business directories.

There is a good chance the last drone shot you saw of a Philippine beach, a Cebu skyline, or a cousin’s wedding was filmed on a DJI. The company makes roughly nine out of every ten consumer drones sold on earth. It started in 2006 in a university dorm room in Hong Kong, built by a student who was, by his own account, a mediocre one. Here is how DJI got here, who actually owns it, why the United States has effectively shut it out, and what any of that means if you are flying one in the Philippines. Who owns DJI? DJI is privately held. It has never listed on a stock exchange, which is unusual for a company its size. The founder, Frank Wang (Wang Tao), is still the chairman and CEO, and he remains the controlling shareholder. The rest is spread across institutional investors that bought in during DJI’s growth years, including the Singapore sovereign wealth fund GIC, New China Life Insurance, New Horizon Capital, Shanghai Venture Capital, and China Chengtong Holdings Group. DJI raised around $500 million in 2015 and about $1 billion in 2018, the latter widely read at the time as IPO preparation. That listing never came. Is DJI a Chinese company, and is it state-owned? It is Chinese. DJI is headquartered in Shenzhen, in a building it calls DJI Sky City, and Shenzhen is where most of its engineering and manufacturing sits. The state-ownership question is the one worth being precise about, because it is where most of the argument about DJI actually lives. DJI describes itself as private but partly state-owned. By its own accounting, state-affiliated investors hold less than 6 percent of the company and less than 1 percent of the voting rights. Whether that is a meaningful amount depends entirely on who you ask. DJI’s position is that a sub-6 percent passive stake with almost no voting power does not give Beijing control of anything. The counter-argument, made by US legislators and defense officials, is that Chinese national security law can compel cooperation from Chinese companies regardless of their cap table, so the percentage is beside the point. Both of those are arguments about law and intent, not about a discovered backdoor. No US agency has published a finding that DJI drones were caught exfiltrating data. Keep that distinction in mind for the ban section further down, because a lot of coverage blurs it. This is also not a DJI-only question. It is the same question that follows TCL into Philippine living rooms and the BBK phone brands into Philippine pockets. The difference is that a drone flies, carries a camera, and records where it has been, which is why DJI draws the scrutiny the others do not. How did DJI start? Frank Wang was born in 1980 in Hangzhou. He was obsessed with flight as a kid, particularly model helicopters, and he was not a strong student. He enrolled at East China Normal University to study electrical engineering and left. He transferred to the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, which is where the actual story begins. For his final-year project he built a flight-control system for a helicopter, the part that keeps an aircraft stable in the air without a human constantly correcting it. He threw everything at it, skipped classes, worked until five in the morning, and the project did not fully work on demo day. He did not get the grade he wanted. What he did get was a professor who saw something in the work and backed him into a graduate program. He later defended a master’s thesis in 2011 on control systems for autonomous helicopters. In the meantime he posted his flight-control results online, found two people who cared, and in January 2006 the three of them started DJI. He built the early prototypes in his dorm room. Later that year they moved to Shenzhen and rented a small apartment to work out of. There were no consumer drones yet. There was no consumer drone market. DJI’s first business was selling flight-control components at around $6,000 a unit to Chinese universities and state-owned power companies, who used them for research and for inspecting infrastructure. Wang has been blunt about how small his ambitions were: he said the idea was to make the product, feed a team of 10 to 20 people, and have a company. He did not know the market could be big, because it did not exist. The part where it almost did not work By 2007, roughly a year in, Wang’s co-founders had left. The team he had built had largely walked out. This is consistently attributed to Wang himself, who is described even in friendly write-ups as abrasive and a perfectionist, and whose standards produced brutal staff turnover in the early years. What saved the company was not a venture fund. It was a family friend named Lu Di, who put in roughly $90,000 and then stayed on to actually manage DJI’s finances, which Wang was not doing. It is worth sitting with that for a second. The company that would go on to take most of the world’s drone market was, at that point, one person with a product, no team, and money from someone who knew his family. You will find a version of this story online involving a stolen design, a lawsuit Wang could not afford, and a professor writing a cheque for 70,000 yuan. Treat that one carefully. The well-sourced version is Lu Di and the $90,000. The rest circulates mostly through aggregator blogs quoting each other. Things turned in 2009. DJI released a flight controller called the XP3.1, and separately, footage shot over Mount Everest using DJI stabilisation put the company in front of a global audience for the first time. In 2010 Wang brought in a high school friend, Swift Xie Jia, to run marketing, which mattered more than it sounds, because DJI’s problem was never engineering. In 2011 he set up DJI North America with Colin Guinn. What the drone market looked like before the Phantom It is worth stopping here to picture the landscape DJI was about to walk into, because the Phantom looks obvious in hindsight and was not obvious at all. The first consumer drone was not a DJI. It was the Parrot AR.Drone, launched in 2010 by a French company, and it was essentially a toy: you flew it from your phone, it was light, it was fun, and it was not a camera platform. Above that sat the DIY scene, hobbyists on forums assembling quadcopters from parts, and above that sat 3D Robotics in Berkeley, which was the most credible Western drone company in the world at the time and was run by Chris Anderson, the former editor of Wired. DJI was none of those things. It was a components supplier selling flight controllers and gimbals to the DIY crowd and to universities. It was upstream of the market, not in it. The specific thing the Phantom 1 added in 2013 was GPS position hold. Before that, a drone did not know where it was. Let go of the sticks and it drifted, so flying one meant constantly correcting it, and filming with one meant flying it well enough to think about the shot at the same time. The Phantom could hold its own position in the air. That is what turned a piloting skill into a camera. How the Phantom changed everything In 2013 DJI released the first Phantom at $629, and this is the hinge of the entire story. Before the Phantom, flying a camera drone meant assembling one. You bought a frame, motors, a flight controller, a gimbal, a transmitter, and a camera, and you made them work together. It was a hobby with a steep and expensive learning curve, which is exactly why almost nobody did it. The Phantom arrived in a box, ready to fly, at a price a serious hobbyist could justify. DJI had spent seven years building the hard part, the flight control, and then wrapped it in something a person could use on the first afternoon. That is the whole trick. DJI did not invent the drone. It removed every reason not to own one. The market it created then belonged to it. By 2015 DJI passed $1 billion in revenue and shipped the Phantom 3. In 2017 it won a Technology and Engineering Emmy for camera drone work in television, and Wang became Asia’s youngest tech billionaire. By 2020 DJI held about 77 percent of the US consumer drone market. As of mid-2024 it held over 90 percent of the consumer drone market worldwide. In 2025 DJI reported revenue of about 80 billion yuan, roughly $11.5 billion. The company has also pushed well past drones into gimbals, action cameras, the Osmo line, and even e-bike motors. What happened to everyone who tried to compete The interesting part of DJI’s story is not that it won. It is how completely everyone else lost, and how fast. 3D Robotics was the one that was supposed to beat DJI. It was American, well funded, well connected, and in 2015 it launched the Solo as its flagship. The company then made a forecasting error that is now a business school case: it read its own “sell in” numbers, the units shipped into retailers like Best Buy, as if they were “sell through” numbers, the units actually bought by people. Retailers can send stock back. 3D Robotics committed to 60,000 units, then added 40,000 more, on drones that cost over $750 each to build and ship. The holiday season did not deliver. By early 2016 it had closed warehouses, laid off large numbers of staff, and walked away from consumer drones entirely. Parrot , the company that arguably started the category, said in a 2017 filing that it would no longer compete with DJI in consumer. It formally exited consumer drones in July 2019 and moved to enterprise and defense work, where it is still operating. GoPro got the worst of it, and it deserves its own section below, but the short version belongs here. GoPro launched the Karma drone in October 2016. It recalled it roughly 16 days later, about 2,500 units, because some of them lost power in flight and fell out of the sky. GoPro brought Karma back, kept going for another year, and shut the drone business down in January 2018. Reporting at the time put the cost of the whole detour at more than $200 million across three years. So within about five years of the first Phantom, the most credible American challenger had collapsed, the European pioneer had retreated to enterprise, and the biggest action camera brand on earth had set fire to $200 million and left. That is the context for the market share numbers. DJI did not edge out a field. The field vacated. How DJI took the camera market too: the Osmo era Here is the part that gets missed when DJI is filed away as “the drone company.” Some of its most successful products do not fly. DJI’s core competence was never really aviation. It was keeping a camera steady while the thing holding it moves. That is what a gimbal does, and a gimbal does not care whether it is bolted to an aircraft or held in a hand. Once DJI understood that, the Osmo line followed, and it walked straight into GoPro’s business. The Osmo Pocket 3 , launched in October 2023, is the clearest example. It is a small handheld camera on a motorised gimbal with a flip-out screen, built for one person filming themselves. It became a genuine cultural object. It has passed 10 million units sold. At one point it took over 34 percent of the entire video camera market in Japan, which is not a market that hands share to newcomers. Related content on Chinese social platforms passed 1.2 billion views. It sold out repeatedly for more than a year after launch, and it kept selling even in the US after tariffs pushed the price from $519 to $799. The reason is the creator economy, and the timing was not luck. The Pocket 3 arrived exactly as short-form vertical video became the default way people make things, and it solved the specific problem of the solo creator. One person, no crew, no tripod, walking and talking, needs stabilisation and needs to see themselves. There was no clean answer to that before. It became close enough to a default that it is routinely described as the industry standard for solo creators. The Osmo Action line did the same thing to GoPro’s home category more directly, by matching the format and undercutting the price. It worked. Across the first three quarters of 2025, DJI held about 66 percent of the action camera market, passing GoPro to become number one in the category GoPro invented. If you are in the Philippines, this is the part of DJI that probably matters most to you day to day. A handheld camera carries none of the regulatory weight a drone does. No registration question, no airport radius, no daylight restriction, no geofencing refusing to let you start. You just film. The collapse of GoPro GoPro is the clearest measure of what DJI did, so it is worth following to the end. In 2014 GoPro was the story. It went public, the stock passed $93, and it had effectively created the action camera. Nick Woodman had built one of the great consumer hardware brands from selling camera straps out of a van. The decline was not a single event. The Karma drone failure in 2016 and 2017 was the visible wound, but the deeper problem was that GoPro stayed a camera company while DJI became a stabilisation company that also made cameras. Then the phones got good enough for casual users, and the Osmo line took the serious ones. The numbers are stark. Revenue was above $1 billion in 2023, $801.5 million in 2024, and $651.5 million in 2025. First quarter 2026 revenue fell about 26 percent year on year to roughly $99 million while losses widened. The company said publicly there was substantial doubt it could survive another twelve months. In July 2026 Nasdaq warned it about delisting after 30 straight days below the $1 minimum bid, and the stock that once cleared $93 was trading around 80 cents. That same month Woodman put $20 million of his own money in to keep the lights on while he looked for a buyer. He found one. On September 2, 2026, GoPro announced that Starman Optical, a privately held US optics company, would acquire 90 percent of it for $285 million, about $1.14 a share, with roughly $92 million of GoPro debt repaid at closing and existing shareholders left with around 10 percent. The plan is to point GoPro’s optics patents, more than 2,500 of them, at defense, government, robotics, and aerospace, and to move production of critical optical components back to the United States. GoPro says it will keep supporting existing consumer products. Read that sequence next to the other one. The American company that invented the category ends up sold for its patents and repositioned as a defense supplier, while the Chinese company that took the category ends up on a US national security list. Those are not two unrelated stories. They are the same story from the two ends. Insta360, the one competitor that is actually winning something There is exactly one company giving DJI a real fight right now, and it is not American or European. It is from the same city. Insta360, formally Arashi Vision, was founded in Shenzhen in 2015 by Liu Jingkang, known as JK Liu. It went after a niche DJI had left alone, the 360 degree camera, and owned it. By 2023 it held roughly two thirds of the consumer 360 camera market. In 2024 it did about 5.6 billion yuan in revenue, around $780 million, up more than 53 percent in a year, with roughly three quarters of that coming from outside China. In June 2025 it listed on Shanghai’s STAR Market. The shares closed day one up nearly 285 percent, valuing the company around $9.9 billion and making Liu a billionaire at 33. DJI responded the way DJI responds. On July 31, 2025, it launched the Osmo 360, matching the Insta360 X5 on headline specifications, 8K panoramic video and 120 megapixel stills, and pricing it at 2,999 yuan, exactly 800 yuan under the X5. Insta360 saw it coming and cut the X5 by 500 yuan roughly two hours before DJI’s launch event, which is not something a market leader does casually. It did not hold. Within about three months DJI had taken roughly 49 percent of the Chinese e-commerce channel for 360 cameras against Insta360’s 47 percent, in a category Insta360 had owned outright. The honest read on Insta360 is that it is the healthiest competitor DJI has faced and it is still losing ground in its own category. That tells you something about how hard DJI is to fight even when you are good, well funded, fast, and operating out of the same talent pool in the same city. Why is DJI banned in the US? This is the live story, and most of what is written about it is wrong in one direction or the other, so here is the sequence. The 2025 National Defense Authorization Act did not ban DJI. It did something more like a countdown. It required a US national security agency to complete a formal security audit of DJI within one year. If no agency completed that audit, DJI would be added to the Federal Communications Commission’s Covered List by default. No agency completed the audit.
